query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Under high‐temperature oxidation conditions, the dual nanoprecipitates in additive‐manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA undergo dynamic elemental redistribution that facilitates the formation of a protective oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: Additive‐manufactured dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a baseline distribution of Ti-, Cr-, and other alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Application of an in situ high-resolution TEM examination with concurrent EDS/EELS mapping during controlled high-temperature oxidation.
generation.conditions: Real-time oxidation at service-simulating high temperatures (with controlled oxygen partial pressure and temperature ramps) replicating gas turbine or aerospace operational environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoprecipitate morphology and their elemental composition at nanoscale
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature oxidation, oxygen ingress triggers preferential oxidation of certain alloying elements within nanoprecipitates; this drives compositional shifts (e.g., enrichment or depletion of Ti, Cr, or Al) at the precipitate-matrix interfaces, promoting the development of a protective, continuous oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: In situ TEM with EDS/EELS mapping will reveal real-time dynamic changes in the nanoprecipitate elemental distribution and morphology, correlated with the formation and growth of a protective oxide at the nanoprecipitate interfaces, which is expected to mitigate further oxidation degradation.
generation.baseline: Ex situ post-oxidation analyses that capture only static snapshots of oxide layers and nanoprecipitates may miss these dynamic redistribution processes.
generation.boundary: The observed dynamic effects are expected to be significant only under high-temperature oxidation and controlled oxygen partial pressures; at lower temperatures or non-replicative conditions, the redistribution may be minimal or undetectable.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics and the extent of elemental redistribution remain uncertain due to the complex interplay of oxidation kinetics and nanoprecipitate stability; variations in local chemistry may also influence the protective nature of the oxide layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare specimens of additive-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA and perform in situ TEM analysis during a controlled high-temperature oxidation experiment. Use a heating stage with adjustable oxygen partial pressure to mimic service conditions. Continuously record TEM images and acquire time-resolved EDS/EELS elemental maps of select nanoprecipitates as the temperature is ramped.
measurements: Real-time TEM imaging of nanoprecipitate morphology changes.
EDS/EELS maps capturing elemental distribution over time.
Measurement of the thickness and continuity of the developing oxide layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ TEM experiments do not show any significant dynamic change in the elemental distribution and morphology of nanoprecipitates, or if no correlated formation/growth of a protective oxide layer is observed during the high-temperature oxidation, then the hypothesis that elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates mediates oxidation resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
